definition: A ballot submitted by a voter who is unable to appear at their assigned polling station on Election Day, typically mailed in advance.
A proposed law, constitutional amendment, or policy question placed on the ballot for voters to approve or reject directly.
Involving cooperation between two major political parties, especially in crafting legislation or policies.
A meeting of party members to select candidates or decide policy, as an alternative to a primary election.
The official process of confirming and declaring election results as valid and final by authorized election authorities.
A geographic area whose voters elect a representative, also called a district, riding, or electorate depending on the country.
A person chosen to represent others at a political convention, often pledged to support a specific candidate.
The revocation or denial of a person's right to vote, whether through legal restrictions or practical barriers.
The process of voting before the official Election Day, typically during a designated early voting period at specific locations.
The system used in the United States where voters choose electors who then formally elect the president. 270 of 538 votes needed to win.
The official register of people eligible to vote in a particular jurisdiction, also called the voter register or voter roll.
A survey conducted with voters immediately after they have cast their ballots, used to project election results.
An electoral system where the candidate with the most votes wins, regardless of whether they achieve a majority (over 50%).
The manipulation of electoral district boundaries to favor a particular political party, named after Governor Elbridge Gerry in 1812.
A process allowing citizens to propose new laws or constitutional amendments by collecting a required number of signatures.
A voting system where ballots are automatically mailed to all registered voters, who can return them by mail or at drop-off locations.
Elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, primarily for congressional seats in the United States.
A strong supporter of a specific political party or cause, or something showing clear political bias toward one party.
The designated location where voters go to cast their ballots on Election Day, typically schools, community centers, or government buildings.
The smallest geographic unit for organizing elections, typically containing one polling station serving nearby residents.
A preliminary election where political party members vote to select their party's candidates for the general election.
An electoral system where seats are allocated to parties based on their share of the total vote, ensuring proportional representation.
A ballot cast when a voter's eligibility is uncertain, held aside until verified before being counted in the final tally.
A voting system where voters rank candidates by preference. If no candidate gets a majority, the lowest is eliminated and votes redistributed.
A re-tabulation of votes cast in an election, triggered by close margins or allegations of counting errors.
The process of redrawing electoral district boundaries, typically after a census, to reflect population changes.
A direct vote by the electorate on a specific proposal or policy question, such as a constitutional amendment or treaty.
A second election held when no candidate achieves the required threshold in the first round, typically between the top two candidates.
The right to vote in political elections. Universal suffrage means all adult citizens have the right to vote regardless of gender, race, or wealth.
A state where both major parties have similar levels of support, making the outcome uncertain and highly contested.
Voting for candidates from different political parties for different offices on the same ballot.
The percentage of eligible voters who actually cast ballots in an election, a key measure of democratic participation.
Identification documents required to verify a voter's identity at the polling station, varying by jurisdiction from photo ID to signature verification.
A candidate whose name is not printed on the ballot but is written in by voters, with varying requirements by jurisdiction.
The systematic process of reviewing and verifying vote tallies after an election, conducted by a canvassing board before certification.
An alliance of political parties formed to create a majority government, common in proportional representation systems.
A public acknowledgment by a losing candidate that they have lost the election, though not legally required in most democracies.
Political spending by organizations that are not required to disclose their donors, often through nonprofit groups.
A legislative tactic used to delay or prevent a vote by extending debate, commonly associated with the United States Senate.
A gerrymandering technique that concentrates opposing voters into a few districts to reduce their influence in surrounding districts.
